Anishinabewaki is the homeland of the Anishinaabe, a family of Algonquian-speaking peoples around the Great Lakes, among them the Ojibwe, Odawa, Potawatomi, Algonquin and Mississauga. Their stories tell of a migration from the Atlantic coast westward along the St. Lawrence and the lakes, guided by a sacred shell.

They lived by hunting, fishing, gathering wild rice and making maple sugar, and travelled by birchbark canoe. From the 1600s they were central to the fur trade of New France, and the Ojibwe, Odawa and Potawatomi formed the Council of Three Fires. In the 1700s and 1800s the Ojibwe spread west into Minnesota and the northern plains, pushing back the Dakota.

Treaties with Britain, Canada and the United States in the 1800s took most of the land, leaving reserves and reservations on both sides of the border, where many Anishinaabe still live. The Caldwell First Nation is one of these communities.
